title: A 1 ATR stop made 7.8% on SPY in 25 years and a 3 ATR stop made 92.1%
author: person-person12
selftext:
Every risk video says the same thing about stops. Keep them tight and cut the loser fast. I had never seen one strategy run with nothing changed except how far away the stop sits, so i ran it three times on SPY daily candles from January 2001 to the end of March 2026, ten grand each, commission and slippage charged on both sides of every fill.

The entry is identical all three times. Buy at the close the day SPY closes above its highest high of the last 50 candles, target 3x the 14 day average true range. The only thing that moves between the three runs is the stop distance.

**1 ATR stop:** 167 trades, 30.5% wins, profit factor 1.06, **+7.8%**, max drawdown 17.2%

**2 ATR stop:** 135 trades, 47.4% wins, profit factor 1.22, **+41.7%**, max drawdown 22.3%

**3 ATR stop:** 125 trades, 60.0% wins, profit factor 1.41, **+92.1%**, max drawdown 21.6%

The tight version **lost 7 trades out of every 10** with the same entries and the same targets as the one that won 6 out of 10. Nothing about the idea got better as the stop widened, the stop just stopped sitting inside normal daily noise. It also took 42 more trades than the 3 ATR version, because getting knocked out early puts you back in cash in time to catch the next breakout.

**\_\_\_\_**

The part i genuinely did not expect is the drawdown column. Tight stops are sold as the thing that buys you a smoother ride, and the 1 ATR run came in at 17.2% against 21.6% on the widest one. **You gave up 84 points of return to save 4.4 points of drawdown.**

Its like braking every time the car ahead of you taps his lights. You never hit anybody and you also never get anywhere.

One entry, one ticker, over a window where the ticker went up roughly 5x, and giving a long position room to breathe is going to flatter itself in that environment. Run the same test on a short side or on something that spent the decade chopping sideways and i would not assume the ranking holds. I ran all three in [Agenticks](https://www.agenticks.ca/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=autopilot&utm_content=ai_trading) off the same 6,347 daily candles so the costs and fills are identical between them, and the only difference between 7.8% and 92.1% is one number in the stop line.
